findings.claim: A period roughly 3000–1200 BC defined by the widespread use of bronze for tools and weapons.
findings.truth: For this Greek unit, the Late Bronze Age is the final phase of the Bronze Age, roughly 1600–1100 BC, when Mycenaean civilisation flourished.
findings.evidence: University of Cambridge, Digital Mycenae (fetched): Mycenaean Late Bronze Age c.1600–1100 BCE; OCR J199 section 2c.

findings.claim: Archaeologists distinguish between Troy VI (destroyed around 1300 BC, possibly by earthquake) and Troy VIIa (destroyed around 1260–1240 BC, possibly by warfare, based on Mycenaean pottery evidence), and debate which — if either — was Homer’s Troy.
findings.truth: Troy VI was destroyed around 1300 BC, probably by an earthquake. Troy VIIa belongs to c.1300–1180 BC and its destruction is placed around 1180 BC; whether that destruction was warfare remains debated.
findings.evidence: British Museum, Troy VI–VIIa guide (fetched); Archaeology Magazine, Troy VII (fetched).

findings.claim: The walls at Mycenae range from six to eight metres thick and up to twelve metres high in places.
findings.truth: The walls average about six metres thick and reach eight metres in places, but their original height is unknown; it has been estimated at about eighteen metres.
findings.evidence: UNESCO Mycenae and Tiryns nomination dossier, pp. 12–13 (fetched).

findings.claim: Every major Mycenaean palace known to archaeologists — at Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos and Knossos — shares the same core design.
findings.truth: Knossos is primarily a Minoan palace, although Mycenaeans settled there after 1450 BC. The comparable mainland palaces here are Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos.
findings.evidence: Hellenic Ministry of Culture, Knossos and Mycenae pages (fetched).

findings.claim: The dagger blade showing a hunting scene depicts lions pursuing spotted deer while hunters advance from the other end.
findings.truth: The prescribed Lion Hunt Dagger from Shaft Grave IV shows four hunters confronting a lion; one hunter has fallen.
findings.evidence: American School of Classical Studies at Athens archive, NM 394 (fetched); University of Strasbourg archaeological study of the Lion Hunt Dagger (fetched).

findings.claim: The gold rhyton from Grave Circle A is a smooth, undecorated conical vessel.
findings.truth: The prescribed gold rhyton from Grave Circle A is a lion’s-head vessel.
findings.evidence: American School of Classical Studies at Athens archive identifies the Mycenae object as a gold lion rhyton, NM 273 (fetched).

findings.claim: The gold pyxis from Shaft Grave V is a small round gold box decorated only with running spirals.
findings.truth: It is a hexagonal wooden box covered with gold plates. Its decoration includes lions attacking herbivores, cattle heads and spirals.
findings.evidence: University of Strasbourg archaeological study, fig. 4 and discussion of the gold plates from the wooden pyxis (fetched).

findings.claim: The Warrior Vase shows two rows of marching soldiers facing each other.
findings.truth: Its two sides show linked scenes: soldiers marching in battle gear while a woman bids them farewell, then soldiers attacking with raised spears.
findings.evidence: National Archaeological Museum, The face of farewell (fetched).

findings.claim: The dromos was cut into the hillside and could be up to thirty metres in length at major tombs.
findings.truth: A dromos could exceed thirty metres: the Tomb of Clytemnestra has a 37-metre dromos.
findings.evidence: UNESCO Mycenae and Tiryns nomination dossier, p. 18 (fetched).

findings.claim: Schliemann famously announced that he had “gazed upon the face of Agamemnon.”
findings.truth: The exact alleged telegram is not securely established. An ASCSA Hesperia article reports that the surviving documentation does not show that Schliemann originally associated this particular mask with Agamemnon.
findings.evidence: Oliver Dickinson, The “Face of Agamemnon”, Hesperia 74 (2005), American School of Classical Studies at Athens (fetched).

findings.claim: Homer’s description includes a “polished stone threshold”, “tall doors” and “mixing bowls brimming with wine”.
findings.truth: No fetched translation verified those exact quotations. The permitted Kline translation of Book 21 has “polished doors” and bowls “brim full of drink”, rather than the quoted wording.
findings.evidence: A. S. Kline, Odyssey Book 21, Poetry in Translation (fetched); OCR J199 names Kline as a permitted translation.

findings.claim: Tomb type directly states a person’s social status: cists were for ordinary people, shaft graves for the elite and tholoi for the greatest rulers.
findings.truth: Option A: remove the fixed status labels and teach tomb form as evidence to evaluate. Option B: retain only qualified wording: tholoi are high-investment and often elite, but chamber tombs span social groups and scholarship questions treating cists and pits as a separate poor class.
findings.evidence: Cambridge University Press, Social Change across the End of the Aegean Bronze Age (fetched), on variation within and between tomb types.
findings.ruling: Option B: qualified wording in prose, cist definition and takeaway.

findings.claim: The gold death mask demonstrates that preserving the identity or physical appearance of the deceased was an established Mycenaean belief.
findings.truth: Option A: recast this throughout as a possible interpretation. Option B: remove it from answer guidance and focus on securely observable facts: the mask was gold, placed over a face and found in an elite shaft grave. The religious meaning cannot be established from the object alone.
findings.evidence: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Mask of Agamemnon (fetched), documents masks laid over faces but does not establish their religious meaning.
findings.ruling: Option A: recast as one interpretation in prose, flashcard and both mark schemes.

summary: Nine verified factual errors require 27 surgical edits, concentrated in prescribed material sources. Two broader interpretive issues are referred for adjudication, and two unverifiable quotations are recorded as notes.
